title: The Network Era
objective: After this level you can explain how three national networks shaped what nearly all Americans watched from the 1950s to the 1970s.
summary: Four networks began regular schedules in 1948; DuMont folded, and ABC, CBS and NBC shaped what nearly everyone watched. By the late 1970s they held over 90 percent of prime time.

cards.headline: Three channels, nearly everybody watching
cards.body: In the late 1970s, more than 90 percent of the US prime-time audience was watching ABC, CBS or NBC. Three companies, one country's evenings. How did television end up with so few doors to walk through?

cards.headline: Four networks, then three
cards.body: Regular programming on the four networks, ABC, CBS, NBC and DuMont, was scarce until the fall of 1948. DuMont folded in the mid-1950s, leaving three. Their battleground was prime time, the evening block from 8 to 11 PM Eastern. Three networks splitting three hours a night: that was the whole menu.

cards.headline: One night, 70 million viewers
cards.body: By 1960 nearly 90 percent of American homes had a television. On September 26 that year, the first televised presidential debate, between John F. Kennedy and Richard Nixon, was carried on all three networks at once and reached a then-record audience of about 70 million. With every channel showing the same event, the country watched together.

cards.headline: Cultural glue
cards.body: Britannica calls broadcasting a kind of cultural glue: from 1929 to 1989, nearly the whole country, young and old, rich and poor, fed from the same cultural trough. Control of television by three companies produced a unified mass culture that nearly everyone experienced. Three choices meant one shared screen.

cards.headline: The network era: shared
learned: ABC, CBS, NBC and DuMont; DuMont folded

questions.prompt: Which of the four TV networks running in 1948 folded in the mid-1950s?

options.label: NBC
options.rationale: NBC survived as one of the big three.

options.label: CBS
options.rationale: CBS survived as one of the big three.

options.label: ABC
options.rationale: ABC survived as one of the big three.

questions.explanation: DuMont folded in the mid-1950s, leaving ABC, CBS and NBC.

questions.prompt: How could one 1960 presidential debate reach about 70 million people?

options.label: It was shown in movie theaters across the country
Nearly 90 percent of homes had TV, and all three networks carried it at once
It was repeated every night for a week
options.rationale: The record was set by a single broadcast.

options.label: It ran only on public television
options.rationale: Public TV didn't exist yet; the three networks carried it.

questions.explanation: With TV in nearly 90 percent of homes and the debate simulcast on all three networks, almost everyone could watch.

questions.prompt: By 1930, eight studios made 95 percent of American films (Level 42). What was television's version of that grip by the late 1970s?

options.label: Three networks drew more than 90 percent of the prime-time audience
Eight studios made all TV shows
options.rationale: The level describes three networks, not studios.

options.label: One public network carried every show
options.rationale: ABC, CBS and NBC were commercial networks.

options.label: Cable channels held most viewers
options.rationale: Cable's rise came later and ended the grip.

questions.explanation: Like the studios, a few companies dominated: ABC, CBS and NBC held over 90 percent of prime time in the late 1970s.
